ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial academic-video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns outside the presentations and long, structured monologues during talks. Early conversation is highly informal and overlap-heavy: people greet late arrivals, make side comments, repeat words, self-correct, and use fillers such as “yeah,” “um,” “okay,” and “all right.” Speech is often fragmented or telegraphic, especially in casual chat and transitions. Formality rises for introductions and presentations, though speakers still hedge frequently with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “likely,” “we’re interested in,” and “I would say.” Participants build on one another through affirming responses before questions—“great talk,” “interesting,” “awesome”—then ask exploratory, multi-part questions rather than sharply challenging claims. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, alternative interpretations, or open questions. Questions commonly begin with softeners (“I have a naive question,” “just curious,” “do you think”) and often include self-repairs or clarification mid-sentence. The moderator uses brief procedural cues to manage transitions, while the group ends with warm thanks and informal follow-up invitations.

Meeting style for this meeting (polite_friction): Courteous but with real tension. People disagree in an indirect way: with a question, a hedge, a long pause, or 'let's take that offline'. Some disagreements are dropped rather than resolved. Nobody raises their voice.

Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Reducing 30-day hospital readmissions for older adults with heart failure after they go home.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a geriatric cardiologist and hospital-based outcomes investigator with 13 years of experience caring for adults with heart failure and leading pragmatic randomized studies. Her work combines electronic health record phenotyping, medication reconciliation audits, guideline-directed medical therapy review, and 30-day all-cause readmission measurement. She has worked closely with discharge nurses and pharmacists and is attentive to how frailty, renal dysfunction, polypharmacy, prior admissions, and illness severity shape post-discharge risk.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats the central question as one of causal attribution: whether receiving the support program changes readmission risk relative to what would have happened under usual discharge processes. For the limited-capacity first six months, she favors individual random assignment among eligible patients, with immediate program access for the intervention group and usual care for controls. In her view, randomization is the most credible protection against selection differences in baseline severity, prior utilization, medication complexity, and unmeasured clinical risk. She recognizes that observation and interviews can identify implementation failures, burdens, and inequities, but argues they cannot by themselves establish that the program caused a reduction in readmissions.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Nia Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is a medical sociologist with 11 years of experience studying care transitions, aging, and unequal access to institutional support. She has conducted longitudinal interviews, home-based ethnographic observation, caregiver network mapping, and qualitative analysis with older adults managing chronic illness after hospitalization. Her prior work examines how household arrangements, unpaid caregiving, language access, neighborhood resources, and trust in hospitals influence whether discharge plans can actually be carried out.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Okafor views post-discharge support as a relational intervention whose effects depend on the household and organizational context in which it is delivered. She proposes a phased rollout by discharge week, paired with observation and interviews of patients, caregivers, and staff, so the team can see how navigation is enacted differently across caregiving configurations and communities. She worries that individual randomization may damage trust and caregiver cooperation when people in the same community discover that some receive navigation while others do not. She explicitly acknowledges that a time-based rollout can be confounded by changing hospital conditions, including seasonal respiratory illness, staffing turnover, and concurrent discharge-policy changes, but sees qualitative fieldwork as necessary for detecting mechanisms and distributional inequities that outcome data alone can conceal.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Martínez
speakers.background: Dr. Martínez is a health economist with 9 years of experience evaluating hospital payment incentives, transitional-care programs, and value-based purchasing arrangements. He uses claims and hospital utilization data, micro-costing, budget-impact models, and quasi-experimental policy evaluation to estimate program costs and consequences. His work has included analyses of readmission penalties, staffing costs, avoided utilization, and how Medicare and payer contracting rules alter hospitals' incentives to invest in post-discharge care.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Martínez frames the study as both an effectiveness and resource-allocation problem. He does not attempt to settle the allocation dispute between individual randomization and phased rollout; instead, he emphasizes that either approach must prospectively record program delivery intensity, labor and referral costs, and downstream hospital utilization so the team can estimate cost per avoided readmission. He is especially attentive to whether rollout timing coincides with changes in payment models, penalty exposure, or discharge-policy incentives, since those changes could affect both utilization and the apparent economic value of the program.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

benchmark_task: Give a meeting where two disciplines propose conflicting methods for the same step, with credible reasons for both. The evaluated AI must fairly summarize both and explain what problem each method avoids, rather than simply selecting a winner.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where two disciplines propose conflicting methods for the same step, with credible reasons for both. The evaluated AI must fairly summarize both and explain what problem each method avoids, rather than simply selecting a winner.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: During the meeting, have the clinical medicine lead and the sociology lead explicitly disagree about the same design step: how to allocate eligible discharged patients to receive the limited-capacity support program during the first six months. The clinical lead proposes individual random assignment, with the program offered immediately to the intervention group and usual discharge processes for the control group. They state that randomization is needed to make differences in 30-day all-cause readmission attributable to the program rather than baseline illness severity, prior admissions, medication complexity, or other selection differences. The sociology lead proposes a phased rollout by discharge week combined with qualitative observation and interviews of patients, caregivers, and staff. They state that individual randomization can undermine trust and caregiver cooperation when patients in the same community learn that some people receive navigation while others do not, and that a phased approach permits the team to observe whether the program is delivered differently across households and caregiving situations. The sociology lead should acknowledge that time-based rollout can be confounded by changing hospital conditions, such as seasonal respiratory illness, staffing changes, or concurrent discharge-policy changes. The clinical lead should acknowledge that interviews and observation can reveal implementation barriers and inequities but cannot by themselves establish whether the program caused a readmission reduction. The economics lead should not resolve the disagreement; they should note that either design must record program delivery costs and hospital utilization so cost per avoided readmission can be assessed, and that rollout timing may interact with payment-model changes. No final design decision is made in the meeting. Do not state the benchmark task, instruct anyone to summarize, or reveal the intended evaluation criteria to participants.

ground_truth.shared_step_under_dispute: Allocation of eligible older adults with heart failure to a limited-capacity post-discharge support program during the first six months.

clinical_medicine_method.method: Individual random assignment to immediate program access versus usual discharge processes.
clinical_medicine_method.credible_rationale: It creates comparable groups and supports causal estimation of the program's effect on 30-day all-cause readmission.
clinical_medicine_method.problem_avoided: Selection bias and confounding, including the risk that patients who receive support differ systematically in illness severity, prior readmissions, medication complexity, or other baseline risks.

sociology_method.method: Phased rollout by discharge week, paired with qualitative observation and interviews of patients, caregivers, and staff.
sociology_method.credible_rationale: It is more compatible with building trust and caregiver cooperation and allows close study of how household arrangements, caregiving capacity, and implementation conditions shape actual program delivery.
sociology_method.problem_avoided: Loss of trust, perceived unfairness, and altered participation or caregiving behavior that could arise if otherwise similar patients are individually assigned unequal access; it also avoids overlooking implementation differences across households.

acknowledged_limitations.clinical_medicine_method: Randomization does not on its own explain implementation failures, household-level barriers, or unequal delivery; qualitative work is needed for those questions.
acknowledged_limitations.sociology_method: A rollout by time can be confounded by seasonality, staffing changes, concurrent discharge-policy changes, and other temporal differences.

ground_truth.economics_role: Economics notes that both approaches require measurement of program delivery costs and hospital utilization to estimate cost per avoided readmission, and flags that payment-model changes could affect interpretation of rollout-period outcomes.

seed_location: Turns 2-4 establish the sociology lead's phased rollout by discharge week with interviews/observation and acknowledge temporal confounding; turns 13-16 explicitly contrast it with the clinical lead's individual random assignment, with clinical concerns about baseline/weekly differences and sociology's trust, fairness, caregiver-cooperation, and household-delivery concerns. Turn 5 notes secular time confounding and required cost/utilization measurement; turns 17 and 19 further discuss utilization and cost per avoided readmission. transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: …and the discharge list can look completely fine in the chart, but then a pharmacy delay means the patient goes home without the medication anyway. Um, anyway—thanks, everyone. I was hoping today we could get clear on what a first six-month evaluation could realistically look like while staffing is tight, and what we need to capture so 30-day readmissions mean something, rather than just reflecting who happened to get offered help.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: …because being offered help isn't the same as being able to use it at home. I'd phase it in by discharge week instead of assigning people individually, and from the first cohort, I'd build in interviews and some observation with patients, whoever's actually coordinating care, and the discharge staff. Maya, how much can we see before discharge in the clinical data about frailty or medication-management difficulty, and how much only shows up once they're home?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Some of it is visible, like prior admissions, eGFR, number of medications, documented frailty or mobility needs, and whether there’s a caregiver listed. But the practical medication-management difficulty is only partly there. The pharmacy fill problem, who can pick things up, whether somebody understands a changed dose- that often doesn’t show up until after discharge. And that’s why I’m hesitant about a week-by-week rollout. Even if we capture covariates well, the weeks can differ in acuity and discharge conditions in ways we won’t see.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: And I don’t think fieldwork makes that confounding disappear. But individual assignment would also make the intervention socially uneven, in a way that changes uptake itself. Could we treat the discharge-week rollout as a pragmatic implementation study, document unit staffing, respiratory volume, and any policy shifts each week, then, um, see whether there’s enough household variation within and across waves before we lock the design?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: …I think that documentation is necessary, but it won't fully repair a secular rollout comparison if discharge conditions are moving with calendar time. For the economic endpoint, we also need prospective service-use data—reconciliation actually completed, successful call attempts, repeated pharmacy or home-service coordination, referral costs—not just an offer flag, or cost per avoided readmission will be uninterpretable. Maya, are those delivery fields recorded consistently enough to separate delivered from offered care?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Some of it is there, but not reliably in structured fields. We can pull reconciliation completion and call attempts, though pharmacy coordination and whether the patient actually got the changed regimen are often buried in notes or absent. I'd want a small prospective delivery log for every eligible patient. Offered, assigned- actually, we'd log offered, assigned, completed, timing, pharmacy barriers, and referrals, because otherwise even the randomized comparison becomes a black box.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: Mm, the timing piece too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: The log needs a field for who was involved in each contact, not just whether it happened. A completed nurse call can mean something very different if the patient is alone, if an adult child takes over the phone, or if nobody who manages the pills is there. Otherwise we'll misread both “delivery” and engagement.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, that matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: And the log should capture intensity, not just whether something was completed, especially repeated coordination. In prior budget work, the expensive cases were often the few that needed multiple contacts with pharmacies, home services, or family, and diagnosis count didn't predict that very well. Nia, what would you count as something observable that shows the caregiver network is actually carrying the discharge plan, instead of just being listed or present?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: …I'd look for enacted coordination, not a caregiver checkbox. Who knows the changed regimen, who physically obtains it, who gets contacted when there's a problem, and whether those roles are shared, contested, or simply unavailable. We could capture that with a very short network map at discharge and then test it against the call notes. Though I- I'd want to be careful not to treat one named adult child as equivalent to actual caregiving capacity.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: Mm, enacted coordination, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And that’s exactly the kind of thing that can affect whether the intervention works, not just who needs it. I still think for the first six months, we need individual random assignment among eligible patients. Otherwise those networks, plus acuity and staffing week by week, can all get folded into the apparent effect. Nia, have you seen the unequal-help issue land mainly within families, or does it travel through clinic or neighborhood networks too?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: …both, but it travels farther than we tend to assume. Adult children compare discharge experiences through church, apartment buildings, dialysis transport, and clinic waiting rooms, so an individual lottery can start to look arbitrary pretty quickly, especially when caregiving is already strained. And within a family, it can create this awkward split over who the hospital seems to recognize as responsible. I’d want to know if we can randomize at a level that doesn’t put near-neighbors into visibly different care pathways, because then…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: …I worry that clustering by neighborhood or clinic makes the allocation less visible, but then we’re right back to baseline differences and a much smaller effective sample. Could we ask the discharge team whether a neutral, capacity-based lottery, explained consistently to everyone, is workable? And have Nia’s interviews specifically track whether that explanation changes trust? I don’t know that it removes the concern, but it lets us, um, measure it instead of assuming it away.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: …I could live with testing that if the explanation is genuinely standardized, and not just a script staff use when there’s time. But I’d want the interviews to include people who weren’t selected too, and caregivers, not only recipients, because the trust effect may show up as withdrawal or resentment before it shows up as a survey response. And I still think we should ask whether the discharge team can, can sustain that explanation on a busy Friday.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: …and from the utilization side, we should log the capacity explanation itself, at least whether it was delivered, who delivered it, and when. If trust or uptake differs after a rushed Friday discharge, that isn't just qualitative context. It can change both the intensity actually delivered and the cost per avoided readmission. I'd also want to see if we can link timely claims or regional feeds for readmissions outside our hospital, because otherwise any allocation comparison is going to miss some of the downstream use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: External readmissions are non-negotiable for the primary outcome. I think we need to confirm what the regional feed captures and its lag before we promise 30-day all-cause readmission. Otherwise, we should be explicit that it's hospital-based use, which is a different endpoint. And that check probably belongs in the discharge-team feasibility conversation too, too, whether they can do the lottery and the standardized explanation without holding people up.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: Before we specify the endpoint, I need to know whether the regional feed is encounter-level and how quickly it arrives, or whether we need claims, which may be too lagged for the six-month analysis. And if external utilization is incomplete, the economic result has to be framed very carefully. Cost per avoided observed readmission is not quite the same thing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hm, that’s a real limitation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: …and if the endpoint has to be hospital-based, the interviews matter even more, because people may be seeking care elsewhere precisely when they don't trust the discharge pathway or can't make the plan work. I'd rather not let an incomplete feed turn those trajectories into "no utilization." We should check the linkage, obviously, but also ask directly about urgent care, outside EDs, and what made them choose them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: We can add a brief 30-day contact with the patient or caregiver about outside ED or hospital use, but I'd treat that as a supplement, not a substitute for the feed, because recall will be uneven. The immediate feasibility checks are probably the linkage and whether discharge staff can actually run a consistent lottery and explanation on a Friday. If either- if either one fails, we need to know before we call this a randomized six-month comparison.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: …yes, and for that feasibility conversation, I’d include one deliberately busy discharge period, not just a normal weekday walkthrough. If the lottery explanation or the network map- if those fall apart under Friday conditions, that tells us something about the intervention’s real organizational setting, not just an implementation glitch.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, especially Friday.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: …and Friday is probably where the economic measurement gets stress-tested too. If the delivery log can't be completed under those conditions, we shouldn't infer zero coordination cost from a blank field. It may just be, um, unrecorded labor. I think the feasibility run needs to distinguish that explicitly, alongside the external-utilization linkage.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Blank has to mean missing, not no work. I’d make that explicit in the feasibility run, with a reason code for an incomplete log, because otherwise Friday missingness could bias both the delivery picture and the randomized comparison. And if we can’t preserve allocation and capture those basics under peak discharge conditions, I don’t think we should... I mean, we shouldn’t pretend the first six months answers the causal question cleanly.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s a high bar.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: …yes. I don't think it's a high bar. It's more like the minimum we need to interpret the result. Otherwise, we could report an attractive cost per avoided readmission, and it could really be an artifact of missing outside utilization or invisible coordination time. I'll check the regional feed and claims timing, and then we can decide if a six-month economic estimate is defensible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should stop there. There’s more, more to sort through, but it can wait until we meet again. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Martínez
transcript.text: All right, take care.

issues: Naturalness is limited by the highly polished, agenda-driven construction of many substantive turns. Disfluencies are present but often feel strategically inserted into otherwise fully formed sentences (for example turns 1, 4, 6, 11, 16, 18, 22, 25, and 26), rather than arising naturally from speakers working through an idea.

This is not enough to reduce task compliance because the benchmark's core requirements are otherwise fully met, but it is a precision gap.
